sections.title: Executive Summary
paragraphs: The Jaggaer INTegration module (JINT) offers both SOAP and REST web-services.
This document aims at describing some general features of JINT webservices, and in particular
1. Overall considerations valid both for SOAP and REST
2. Specific SOAP guidelines applicable to the SOAP interface of all webservices, including
6. Specific REST guidelines applicable to the REST interface of all webservices, including
8. The “grammar” defining query expression to filter resources
9. The authentication methods (based on access token or JWT)
10. Additional security measures and best practices that apply to both REST and SOAP

As general remark, please consider that regardless of the exposed interface (SOAP, REST, CSV, …) the backend services are the same for all the available protocols, so this allows to implement the same integration flows via REST APIs already supported by the other existing protocols.
The list of available web-services and supported protocols (SOAP and/or REST) is defined in the document “JINT Web Services Library and Activation Request” available on JINT SharePoint portal.

Additional details on each single web-service, both for SOAP and REST (e.g. specific resources, endpoints) are defined in the web-service development kit document of each single supported integration flow.

Please note that JINT SOAP web-services and REST APIs are designed to be consumed by the customer system and to transfer data among systems. Provided features, data visibility, authentication approach and other security measures such as anti-DOS filters, are then designed based on this assumption.

sections.title: JINT SOAP Web Services
paragraphs: JINT offers SOAP web-services based on SOAP 11
Each single webservice is defined in a dedicated WSDL file that is includes both the data model (schema) and available endpoints.
Since JINT allows to transfer attachments via webservices, all JINT webservices implements “Message Transmission Optimization Mechanism” (MTOM) over Soap 1.1.
Details are given in the following W3C specification http://www.w3.org/Submission/soap11mtom10.
All SOAP requests including attachments MUST be formatted as MTOM requests.

JINT usually accepts also request including small files encoded base64 and included in the SOAP request but this has not to be considered a feature to be exploited for “production level” integrations since SOAP requests above a preconfigure size threshold (e.g. because including to several or large files encoded in base64) will be refused with a 400 error
JINT SOAP webservices are exposed on a dedicated URL and protected through
1. SSL encryption, i.e. they are exposed on HTTPS
2. IP Filtering, i.e. they are reachable only by the authorized IPs
In addition to this it is possible to implement additional security measures including

sections.title: HTTP Basic [segreto]
paragraphs: At setup time Jaggaer generates username/password to be used by the client component to invoke the SOAP webservices in that specific URL.

JINT supports both pre-emptive and non- pre-emptive authentication but since the security configuration is well known by the client, we strongly recommend adopting the former approach to reduce the number of calls to the webservices endpoint.

Therefore, the client components, in case basic authentication is configured, is required to always send the “authorization” token with the provided credentials (pre-emptive) and not waiting to being challenged for them (non-pre-emptive).

sections.title: SSL Mutual Authentication (SSL Client certificate)
paragraphs: The webservice endpoint is protected by an SSL mutual authentication, therefore the client component is authenticated by the web-service during the SSL handshake

The web service has been designed to manage validation errors related to the SOAP Request content by including error code and error details in the SOAP Response. Possible error codes for each operation are listed in the specific tables in the previous “Error codes” chapters. These errors are not raised at protocol level. This design choice allows errors handling to any legacy system.
The table below describes how the web service responds:

To better manage performances, webservices export responses are limited to a predefined number of items that are configured on a single integration basis (usually it is defaulted to 100 objects per webservice call).

In order to retrieve the full list of objects matching the provided filtering criteria the webservice client must perform multiple calls, one for each “page”. For instance, if an export call retrieves 250 objects and the maximum is set to 100, the webservice client is required to perform 3 webservice calls, one for objects from 1 to 100, one for object from 101 to 200 and the last for the remaining 50 objects.

So, to get the proper subset of results the webservice client can set in the webservice call the parameter startAt (default is 1). Information about how many objects are matching the current export request and how many of them have been returned in the current response are given in the response parameters
1. totRecords: number of objects matching the export criteria
2. returnedRecords: number of objects returned in the current response
3. startAt: index of the first item (it should be exactly what provided in the same parameter of the export request)

sections.title: JINT REST API
paragraphs: As general remark, the REST interface can be considered as an additional interface to expose JINT integration services to customers and partners to be added to already existing SOAP and FTP/CSV interfaces.
The backend services are shared then the REST APIs of a given service can allow to implement the same integration flows supported by the other protocols.
The list of available web-services and supported protocols (SOAP and/or REST) is defined in the document “JINT Web Services Library and Activation Request” available on JINT SharePoint portal.
Additional details on REST APIs for specific webservices (e.g. specific resources, endpoints) are defined in the web-service development kit document of each single supported integration flow.

Please note that REST APIS, as well as other integration interfaces provided by JINT, are designed to be consumed by the customer system and to transfer data among systems. Provided features, data visibility, authentication approach and other security measures such us DOS filters, are then designed based on this assumption.

sections.title: REST API Activation
paragraphs: Rest API are automatically activated once the service is activated for the SOAP interface

Anyways, since this interface implements additional security measures (see Authentication chapter) at activation time it is required to exchange the info required for the setting up of the authentication method required to allow the use of the activated REST APIs.

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: JINT allows to search REST collections by means of a query language based on the standard Feed Item Query Language (FIQL - https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-nottingham-atompub-fiql-00).
The language has been extended to support additional operators and expressions required by JINT services
A query expression (provided in query string parameter) can be composed by several comparison separated by semicolon, representing AND operator
Each comparison is composed by a
1. selector: the field to be applied to the filter
3. the arguments to check the operator against. It can be single or multiple ones.
Allowed selectors and operators depends on each single webservice and filter, will be then available in the specific development kit document.

Argument can be a single value, or multiple values in parenthesis separated by comma. Value that doesn’t contain any reserved character or a white space can be unquoted, other arguments must be enclosed in single or double quotes. If you need to use both single and double quotes inside a quoted argument, then you must escape one of them using \ (backslash). If you want to use \ literally, then double it as \\. Backslash has a special meaning only inside a quoted argument, not in unquoted argument.

sections.title: Attachments support
paragraphs: The REST interface supports the import of files into the Jaggaer platform together with data. Attachments import is supported through multipart POST (multipart/form-data).
1. One parameter with a file representing the JSON payload (the same one used in plain data import); the name of the form parameter must be “data”
2. One or more additional parameters for the files; each parameter must have as name the name given to the file in the JSON payload
E.g. if the JSON references a file named “doc1.pdf” there must be 2 parameters: “data” with the JSON, and “doc1.pdf” with the file. Refer to development kit documents for detailed examples.
Files can be also downloaded through the “attachments” REST API described in the related development kit document.

sections.title: Authentication
paragraphs: As per all JINT webservices REST APIs are protected through
1. SSL encryption, i.e. they are exposed on HTTPS
2. IP Filtering, i.e. they are reachable only by the authorized IPs
In addition to this all REST services are secured by means of additional measures requiring the API client to authenticate itself by means of a Bearer [segreto]
The authentication is always meant to identify the client component, not the end user, since the APIs are designed to transfer data between systems i.e. the J1 platform and customer systems.
Below are described supported tokens and how the authentication process takes places

paragraphs: In order to authenticate itself against the API endpoint can use an opaque token that is provided by the JINT authorization endpoint. Therefore the client components invoke the “Token” API providing some credentials and gets the bearer token to be used to call the APIs.
The access token can be retrieved by the client calling the “tokens” endpoint and providing the credentials communicated at setup phase.

sections.title: JSON Web Token (JWT)
paragraphs: The client component can provide as bearer token in the http header a Signed JWT (JWS). In thi case the token is generated by the client ad used directly to invoke the API endpoint.

JWT standard is defined in RFC7519 (https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7519) while additional information and development guidelines ca be find at https://jwt.io/. Since the JINT approach is similar to the one used by Google to secure its API for service accounts authorization you can find some examples on Google developers site (https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/OAuth2ServiceAccount#jwt-auth).

sections.title: Additional security measures and best practices
paragraphs: This chapter defines some general guidelines that apply both to SOAP and REST services

sections.title: DoS attack protection
paragraphs: In the event the webservice client exceeds a preconfigured number of webservice calls per a given period (usually 100 per minute), when this scenario was not previously agreed, the server will return an HTTP status 429 (Too Many Requests) as per RFC 6585 (https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6585#page-3).
The response will also include the “Retry-After” header indicating how long the client has to wait before making a new request.
In case the client component does ignore or not respect the “Retry-After” such period increases at each call with the result that the server will stop responding.

sections.title: Multiple concurrent calls
paragraphs: We strongly recommend performing sequential calls.

In case of parallel/simultaneous calls, the service puts the requests in a queue and doesn't satisfy a request until the previous ones has been completed. This could lead the client component to experiment a “response timeout” because the request is not server in the expected timeframe.
Each request not satisfied after some time (default is 1 minute) is discharged and an error is returned.
Moreover an high number of parallel calls may activate the protection mechanism against DoS attacks defined in the previous chapter

sections.title: Cookies
paragraphs: All JINT services do not keep any session information then do not require any cookie to work. The client component is then required to not send cookies that could be returned by the previous HTTP request.
In case the client sends some cookie could experiment unexpected responses such us http redirect (302)

The web service exports all fields of type datetime in the installation reference timezone, usually UTC (Universal Time Coordinated) that corresponds to timezone GMT (Greenwich Mean Time). This is evidenced by the date format, for example 2016-03-01T15:30:00.000+00:00, where +00:00 indicates that the offset from UTC is 0.
On the contrary, in the JA User Interface, datetime fields are displayed in the local time of the logged user, i.e. with the timezone associated to the given user.
So, it is possible to experience a time difference (offset) between a datetime field displayed in the JA User Interface and the same one exported by the web service.
For example, a user with CET timezone in the platform will see the dates shifted of 1 or 2 hours (depending on daylight saving time) compared to those exported by the web service in UTC.
The filter condition lastUpdateTime needs to specify the timezone in which the date is expressed, for example 2016-03-01 15:30:00.000 +0100 where +0100 indicates UTC+1.
